Now, as\he Pali was the vernacular language of India from Cuttack to Kapurdagiri within three hundred ycars after the death of S'akya, it would not be unreasonable to suppose that the Gatha, which preceded it, was the dialect of the millions at the time of S'akya's advent and for some time before it, If our conjecture in this respect be right, it would follow that the Sanskrit passed into the Gatha six hundred years before tle Christian era ; that three hundred years subsequently it changed into the Pal; and that thence, in two hundred years more, preceded the Pradkrit and its sister dialects, the' Sapraseni, the Dravidi* and the Panchali, which in their turn formed the present vernacular dialects of India. * Commenting on this word as pvblished in my paper on the ४ Peculiarities of the Gatha Dialect" in the Journal of the Asiatic Society, (XXIII. p. 614). Dr. J. Muir observes ; "if by the Dravidi is meant the Telegu, or any of its cognate languages, it is a mistake to class it with the northern Prakrits." (Sanskrit Texts II, p. 127.) It must be obvious from the manner in which the word has been uscd in the text that a Prakritie dialect is intended, and not the Telegu, nor any of its cognate dialects. That a Prakritic dialect of the kind was once recognised is abundantly evident from the writings of Indian philologists and rhetoricians.
